title: NEC Past Paper - Set 20 (2083 Asoj 17, 3rd shift)

questions.stem: The continuity equation ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0 is valid for flow that is:
questions.solution: **Incompressible, steady or unsteady.** This is the reduced form in which density has cancelled, and only constant density does that. Time does not appear, so steadiness is irrelevant.

examTip.trap: "Steady" is what removes the ∂ρ/∂t term, so it looks like the assumption being made; it is incompressibility that cancels ρ throughout.
examTip.trick: The full form carries ρ in every term. Ask what must be constant to drop it.
examTip.mnemonic: No ρ in sight means incompressible.

questions.stem: The type of aggregate that is rarely available in Nepal is:
questions.solution: **Basalt.** Nepal's geology is Himalayan sedimentary and metamorphic rock. Basalt is volcanic and is not worked here in any quantity.

examTip.trap: Basalt is one of the commonest road aggregates worldwide, so it reads as something available everywhere.
examTip.trick: Ask what the Himalaya is actually made of.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a circle of diameter D about its diametral axis is:
questions.solution: **πD⁴/64.** πD⁴/64 about a diameter. The polar value about the centre is twice that, πD⁴/32.

examTip.trap: πD⁴/32 is the polar moment of inertia, differing only in the denominator.
examTip.trick: J = 2I for a circle, so the diametral value carries the larger denominator.
examTip.mnemonic: 64 about a diameter, 32 about the pole.

questions.stem: The shape factor of a rectangular section is:
questions.solution: **1.5.** Shape factor is the plastic modulus over the elastic modulus: (bd²/4)/(bd²/6) = 1.5.

examTip.trap: 1.0 would mean the section gains nothing from plastic redistribution, which is true of no solid shape.
examTip.trick: Rectangle 1.5, circle 1.7, I-section about 1.12.

questions.stem: The type of surface mining that extracts stone and gravel from the earth is:
questions.solution: **Quarrying.** Quarrying is the open working of rock for building stone and aggregate. Dressing is what is done to the stone afterwards.

examTip.trap: Dressing and blasting are steps in the same industry, but one shapes the stone and the other only loosens it.
examTip.trick: The quarry is the place; quarrying is the working of it.

questions.stem: In Bowditch's rule, the direction of the closing error is given by:
questions.solution: **tan δ = ΣD / ΣL.** The closing error has ΣD in departure and ΣL in latitude, so its bearing is the arctangent of departure over latitude.

examTip.trap: Inverting the ratio gives the complement of the true bearing and looks equally plausible written down.
examTip.trick: Departure is easting, latitude is northing — and a bearing is east over north.

questions.stem: The relation e = wG holds when the soil is:
questions.solution: **Fully saturated.** The general relation is eS = wG. Full saturation makes S = 1 and leaves e = wG.

examTip.trap: A submerged soil is saturated, so that option is not wrong in fact — it simply adds a condition the relation does not need.
examTip.trick: Put S = 1 into eS = wG and see what is left.

questions.stem: The coefficient of passive earth pressure is:
questions.solution: **(1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ).** Passive pressure is the larger of the two, so the larger term goes on top. The active coefficient is its reciprocal.

examTip.trap: The active coefficient is the same expression inverted — the most swapped pair in the subject.
examTip.trick: Kp must exceed 1 and Ka must be below it. Check which way up gives that.
examTip.mnemonic: Passive is big, so plus over minus.

questions.stem: In an M1 profile of gradually varied flow:
questions.solution: **y > y0 > yc.** An M profile lies on a mild slope, so y0 > yc. Zone 1 is above both depths, which gives y > y0 > yc — the backwater curve behind a dam.

examTip.trap: M2, the drawdown curve, is y0 > y > yc: the same three symbols in a different order.
examTip.trick: The number is the zone — 1 above both, 2 between, 3 below both.
examTip.mnemonic: M1 is the backwater, highest of the three.

questions.stem: A stone sinks through a lake. Once fully submerged, the buoyant force on it:
questions.solution: **Remains constant.** Buoyancy equals the weight of fluid displaced, and a fully submerged body displaces its own volume at any depth.

examTip.trap: Pressure does rise with depth, which makes an increasing force feel right — but it rises equally on the top and the bottom.
examTip.trick: The force follows the volume displaced, not the pressure.

questions.stem: The fore poling method of tunnelling is used in:
questions.solution: **Soft ground.** Poles are driven ahead of the face to hold up soft ground while the next length is excavated. Sound rock needs no such support.

examTip.trap: "Poling" sounds like a drilling technique for rock; it is a support technique for ground that will not stand.
examTip.trick: Support ahead of the face is needed only where the face collapses.

questions.stem: The weaving angle at a rotary intersection is generally:
questions.solution: **15°.** Entering and leaving streams cross at about 15°, gentle enough for drivers to merge without stopping.

examTip.trap: A larger angle shortens the weaving length and looks economical, but forces a sharper and more dangerous merge.
examTip.trick: Weaving must be gradual, so the angle is small.
examTip.mnemonic: Weaving angle fifteen degrees, no more.

questions.stem: The carriageway width of a single-lane road is:
questions.solution: **3.75 m.** A single lane is 3.75 m, an intermediate lane 5.5 m and a two-lane carriageway 7.0 m.

examTip.trap: 3.5 m is the width of one lane within a multi-lane carriageway, which is narrower than a road built as a single lane.
examTip.trick: A single-lane road must let a vehicle pull over, so it is wider than a lane in a pair.

questions.stem: The outlet in a dam that releases water downstream according to demand is the:
questions.solution: **Under-sluice.** Sluices are gated outlets operated to meet demand. A spillway passes surplus flood water automatically.

examTip.trap: A spillway also releases water downstream, but only when the reservoir rises above its crest — it answers the flood, not the demand.
examTip.trick: Demand means someone decides, and that needs a gate.
examTip.mnemonic: Sluice for demand, spillway for flood.

questions.stem: The structure built at the head regulator to keep silt out of the canal is the:
questions.solution: **Silt excluder.** An excluder works in the river upstream of the regulator and stops silt entering. An ejector removes silt already in the canal.

examTip.trap: Excluder and ejector differ by one word and by which side of the regulator they stand on.
examTip.trick: Exclude before entry, eject after it.
examTip.mnemonic: Excluder keeps out, ejector throws out.

questions.stem: The Nepal Engineering Council Act was promulgated in:
questions.solution: **2055 BS.** The NEC Act 2055 created the Council; the Regulation followed in 2056.

examTip.trap: 2057 is close enough to be chosen by anyone recalling only the decade.
examTip.trick: Act 2055, Regulation 2056 — consecutive years.

questions.stem: The total number of members of the NEC, including the chairperson, vice-chairperson and registrar, is:
questions.solution: **21.** The Council is constituted of twenty-one members in all under the NEC Act.

examTip.trap: All four are plausible committee sizes, so the figure has to be remembered rather than reasoned.
examTip.trick: Twenty-one, the three office holders included.

questions.stem: The rate of penetration in the CBR test is:
questions.solution: **1.25 mm/min.** The plunger is driven at 1.25 mm per minute, and the loads at 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm penetration are read off.

examTip.trap: 2.5 mm is the first penetration at which a load is read, not the rate at which the plunger moves.
examTip.trick: The rate is in millimetres per minute; the centimetre options are a factor of ten out.

questions.stem: Alligator cracking in a flexible pavement is caused by:
questions.solution: **Fatigue under repeated loading.** Repeated bending puts the underside of the bituminous layer into tension; the crack starts there and works upwards into the interconnected pattern.

examTip.trap: Poor compaction and a bad mix both shorten pavement life, but neither produces this particular pattern.
examTip.trick: The pattern comes from many load cycles, which is what fatigue means.

questions.stem: In a penstock, the friction head loss varies with the velocity as:
questions.solution: **The square of the velocity.** Darcy-Weisbach gives hf = fLv²/(2gD), so doubling the velocity quadruples the loss.

examTip.trap: A linear relation holds only in laminar flow, which a penstock never has.
examTip.trick: The velocity head itself is v²/2g, and friction loss is a multiple of it.

questions.stem: Which grade of bitumen is the hardest?
questions.solution: **30/40.** The numbers are the penetration in tenths of a millimetre, so a lower figure means a stiffer binder.

examTip.trap: A larger number looks like a stronger grade; it means a softer one.
examTip.trick: Penetration measures how far the needle sinks — less is harder.

questions.stem: In a network diagram, the element that consumes neither time nor resources is the:
questions.solution: **Dummy activity.** A dummy shows a dependency only, drawn as a dashed arrow of zero duration.

examTip.trap: An event is also instantaneous, but it is a node rather than an activity.
examTip.trick: The dummy is an arrow that costs nothing.

questions.stem: The minimum percentage of longitudinal reinforcement in an RCC column is:
questions.solution: **0.8%.** IS 456 requires at least 0.8% of the gross area and allows up to 6%, or 4% in practice where bars lap.

examTip.trap: 4% and 6% are the maximum limits from the same clause.
examTip.trick: 0.8 is the floor, 6 the ceiling.

questions.stem: Fixed inorganic solids in a sludge sample are found by igniting it at:
questions.solution: **550 ± 25 °C for 15 minutes.** The volatile fraction burns off at 550 °C and what remains is the fixed inorganic residue.

examTip.trap: The other combinations all look like laboratory conditions; only the temperature and the time together are right.
examTip.trick: Volatile solids leave at 550 °C — the figure to anchor on.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam carries a point load P at mid-span. The central deflection is:
questions.solution: **PL³/48EI.** The standard result for a central point load on a simple span.

examTip.trap: PL³/192EI is the same load on a fixed beam, four times stiffer; PL³/3EI is a cantilever.
examTip.trick: Simple 48, fixed 192, cantilever 3.

questions.stem: For a column fixed at both ends, Euler's critical load is:
questions.solution: **4π²EI/L².** The effective length is L/2 and the load varies inversely with its square, so the basic value is multiplied by four.

examTip.trap: 2π²EI/L² is the fixed-and-hinged case, one step down the same family.
examTip.trick: Multipliers run ¼, 1, 2, 4 as restraint increases.

questions.stem: The ratio of Euler's crippling load for a column with both ends hinged to that with both ends fixed is:
questions.solution: **1/4.** Hinged gives π²EI/L² and fixed gives 4π²EI/L², so the ratio is one to four.

examTip.trap: 4 is the same relation read backwards, and is picked by anyone who inverts the ratio.
examTip.trick: Hinged is the weaker case, so the ratio must be below one.

questions.stem: Lacing bars in a built-up column are inclined to the column axis at:
questions.solution: **40° to 70°.** IS 800 requires the lacing to lie between 40° and 70°, which keeps both the lacing force and the panel length within reason.

examTip.trap: A steeper angle looks better at bracing, but it shortens the panel and multiplies the number of bars.
examTip.trick: Lacing is diagonal, so it sits either side of 45°.

questions.stem: For a single project, net present value and internal rate of return lead to:
options: A decision on cash flow only
questions.solution: **The same accept-or-reject decision.** NPV is positive exactly when the IRR exceeds the discount rate, so for one project the two agree. They can rank competing projects differently.

examTip.trap: The two are famous for disagreeing — but only when ranking mutually exclusive projects, not when judging one.
examTip.trick: NPV > 0 and IRR > i are the same statement.

questions.stem: For less than 5 msa on a single-lane two-way road, the minimum subgrade CBR specified is:
questions.solution: **5%.** Below a CBR of 5% the subgrade must be improved or replaced before a pavement is designed on it.

examTip.trap: The higher figures are sub-base and base course requirements, not subgrade ones.
examTip.trick: The subgrade is the weakest layer allowed, and 5% is its floor.
examTip.mnemonic: Subgrade CBR of at least 5 per cent.

questions.stem: For the same material, the compressive strength of a cube exceeds that of a cylinder by about:
questions.solution: **20%.** Platen friction confines the squat cube and raises its apparent strength; the cylinder reads about 0.8 of the cube value.

examTip.trap: The difference is a property of the specimen shape rather than of the concrete, so it is easy to assume it is larger.
examTip.trick: Cylinder ≈ 0.8 × cube.
examTip.mnemonic: Cube is about a fifth stronger.

questions.stem: The ratio of the base period to the delta gives the:
questions.solution: **Duty.** Duty, delta and base period are tied by Δ = 8.64B/D, so the duty follows from the base period divided by the depth applied.

examTip.trap: Delta appears in the question itself, which makes it the reflex answer.
examTip.trick: Duty is an area per unit discharge — the only one of the four that is a ratio of the other two.
examTip.mnemonic: Base period over delta is duty.

questions.stem: In a guide bank, the maximum scour occurs at the:
questions.solution: **Nose.** The flow is deflected most sharply around the upstream curved head, so velocity and scour are greatest there — which is why the apron is heaviest at the nose.

examTip.trap: The launching apron is where the stone ends up, which makes it look like the point of attack rather than the defence.
examTip.trick: Scour is worst where the flow turns most sharply.
examTip.mnemonic: The nose of the guide bank takes the worst scour.

questions.stem: Waterlogging harms plant growth chiefly by reducing:
questions.solution: **Aeration of the root zone.** Saturated soil has no air in its voids, and roots need oxygen as much as water.

examTip.trap: Microbial activity falls too, but that follows from the same loss of oxygen rather than being the primary harm.
examTip.trick: Water fills the voids that air should occupy.
examTip.mnemonic: Saturated soil has no air, so the roots drown.

questions.stem: In Lacey's regime theory, the velocity of flow is proportional to:
questions.solution: **Silt factor and hydraulic radius.** Lacey's regime relation is V² = (2/5) f R, so velocity follows the silt factor and the hydraulic mean depth.

examTip.trap: Discharge appears in the perimeter and scour relations of the same theory, which makes it look as though it belongs here too.
examTip.trick: Velocity relates to f and R; discharge relates to P and R.
examTip.mnemonic: Lacey velocity: V² = 2fR/5, not a discharge relation.

questions.stem: The equation of a parabolic arch of span L and rise h is:
questions.solution: **y = 4hx(L − x)/L².** The curve must be zero at both springings and equal to h at mid-span, which this form satisfies.

examTip.trap: Changing the sign inside the bracket turns the arch upside down, and the error is invisible until values are substituted.
examTip.trick: Put x = L/2 and check that y comes out as h.
examTip.mnemonic: Parabolic arch: y = 4hx(L − x)/L², zero at both ends.

questions.stem: Arches are used for long-span bridges mainly because they develop:
questions.solution: **A large horizontal thrust.** The horizontal thrust at the supports cancels most of the load-induced moment, so the section carries mainly axial compression.

examTip.trap: Bending moment is what the arch avoids, not what it develops — which is precisely why it spans so far.
examTip.trick: An arch converts bending into compression.

questions.stem: Water flows at 0.8 m/s through a 50 mm pipe, losing 0.5 m of head in 10 m. The friction factor is about:

examTip.trap: Forgetting to divide by the length gives ten times the answer, which lands among the other options.
examTip.trick: Rearrange before substituting: f = 2gD·hf/(L·v²).

questions.stem: In which canal fall does the discharge-stage relationship stay unchanged?
questions.solution: **Trapezoidal notch fall.** The notch is shaped so the depth-discharge relation upstream is preserved, leaving the regime of the canal undisturbed.

examTip.trap: An ogee fall is the smoothest hydraulically, which makes it sound like the one that disturbs the flow least.
examTip.trick: The notch is designed for exactly this property; the others are not.

questions.stem: As a stone enters the water, and before it is fully submerged, the buoyant force:
questions.solution: **Increases.** The submerged volume grows as the stone sinks in, and buoyancy is the weight of the volume displaced.

examTip.trap: Once fully submerged the force becomes constant, and that later stage answers the commoner version of this question.
examTip.trick: Buoyancy follows the submerged volume, which is still growing.
examTip.mnemonic: More in the water, more lift.

questions.stem: For an inclined submerged plane surface, the centre of pressure lies:
questions.solution: **Below the centroid.** Pressure grows with depth, so the resultant acts lower than the geometric centre by I sin²θ/(A·h̄).

examTip.trap: For a horizontal surface the two coincide, and that special case gets remembered as the general rule.
examTip.trick: Greater pressure lower down pulls the resultant down.
examTip.mnemonic: Centre of pressure is always deeper.

questions.stem: In the Moody diagram, the friction factor curves are plotted from:
questions.solution: **The Colebrook-White equation.** Colebrook-White covers the whole transitional and rough turbulent range, and the Moody chart is its graphical form.

examTip.trap: Darcy-Weisbach is the equation the friction factor is used in, not the one it comes from.
examTip.trick: One equation gives f, the other spends it.
examTip.mnemonic: Colebrook gives f, Darcy uses it.

questions.stem: The middle-third rule is applied to ensure that there is no:
questions.solution: **Tension at the base.** Keeping the resultant within the middle third of the base keeps the whole section in compression, which masonry and concrete need.

examTip.trap: Sliding and overturning are the other stability checks, applied to the same base.
examTip.trick: Masonry cannot take tension — that is what the rule protects against.

questions.stem: The demand factor of a power system is:
questions.solution: **Maximum demand ÷ connected load.** Not every connected appliance runs at once, so the maximum demand is always less than the connected load and the factor is below one.

examTip.trap: Average load over maximum demand is the load factor, which is the better-known ratio.
examTip.trick: Demand factor compares demand with what is connected; load factor compares average with peak.

questions.stem: Trash racks are provided mainly to:
options: Keep floating material out of the turbine
questions.solution: **Keep floating material out of the turbine.** A steel grille across the intake stops logs and rubbish reaching the runner, where they would damage the blades.

examTip.trap: A rack does restrict the opening slightly, which makes controlling the opening sound like its purpose rather than a side effect.
examTip.trick: Debris is solid, so the defence is a screen.

questions.stem: The primary function of waste water treatment is:
options: Removing and safely disposing of organic and suspended waste
Removing the hardness of the water
questions.solution: **Removing and safely disposing of organic and suspended waste.** Treatment reduces the organic load and the solids so the effluent can be discharged without destroying the receiving water.

examTip.trap: Producing drinking water is the aim of water treatment; waste water treatment aims at safe disposal.
examTip.trick: Ask which direction the water is going.
examTip.mnemonic: Treat to discharge, not to drink.

questions.stem: The minimum flow velocity in a pressure conduit is kept at about:
questions.solution: **0.6 m/s.** Below about 0.6 m/s suspended matter settles out and the conduit silts up.

examTip.trap: The larger figures are maximum velocities, set to limit friction loss and surge.
examTip.trick: The minimum keeps solids moving; the maximum limits the loss.

questions.stem: The carriageway together with the shoulders on either side, including any median, is the:
questions.solution: **Formation width.** Formation width is the finished top width of the embankment or cutting. The right of way is the whole land reserved, which is wider.

examTip.trap: Right of way is the other width quoted for every road, and the two are constantly interchanged.
examTip.trick: Formation is what is built; right of way is what is owned.

questions.stem: The degree of compaction achieved in the field does NOT depend on:
options: The strength of the parent rock
questions.solution: **The strength of the parent rock.** Compaction depends on the energy applied, the water content and the soil being compacted. What the grains were once part of does not enter it.

examTip.trap: Rock strength governs an aggregate's resistance to crushing, which is a different property from a different test.
examTip.trick: Compaction rearranges grains; it does not break them.

questions.stem: At a grade-separated interchange, a turn through a right angle only is served by a:
questions.solution: **Unidirectional ramp.** A unidirectional ramp carries one movement in one direction and leaves the through carriageway at a right angle.

examTip.trap: A semi-directional ramp also serves one movement, but curves away from and back towards the natural direction of travel.
examTip.trick: One direction, one movement, one ramp.
examTip.mnemonic: Unidirectional ramp: one movement, one direction.

questions.stem: The science of the occurrence, circulation and distribution of water on the earth and in the atmosphere is:
questions.solution: **Hydrology.** Hydrology studies the water itself through the hydrological cycle. Hydraulics studies how it behaves in a conduit or channel.

examTip.trap: Climatology and meteorology also concern the atmosphere, but they study the weather rather than the water.
examTip.trick: Hydro- is water and -logy is its study.

questions.stem: The ultimate bearing capacity of a soil is:
options: The safe load per unit area
The load on the foundation per unit area
The ultimate strength per unit volume
The load intensity at which the soil fails in shear
questions.solution: **The load intensity at which the soil fails in shear.** It is the pressure at which shear failure occurs. Dividing it by a factor of safety gives the safe value used in design.

examTip.trap: "Safe load per unit area" is the safe bearing capacity — the ultimate value already reduced.
examTip.trick: Ultimate means at failure, before any factor of safety.

questions.stem: The triaxial test is preferred mainly because it offers:
options: Control of drainage and confining pressure
questions.solution: **Control of drainage and confining pressure.** Cell pressure and drainage can both be set, so the test reproduces the field condition — UU, CU or CD — far better than a shear box.

examTip.trap: The direct shear box is the cheap and quick test, and the two are compared on exactly these grounds.
examTip.trick: The triaxial's advantage is control, not convenience.

questions.stem: A point of contraflexure is a section at which the:
questions.solution: **Bending moment changes sign.** The curvature reverses and the moment passes through zero, so no moment reinforcement is needed at that section.

examTip.trap: Zero shear marks the maximum moment — the neighbouring and opposite condition.
examTip.trick: Contraflexure is about the moment changing sign, not its size.

questions.stem: Circular dressed stones are generally used for:
questions.solution: **Columns and pillars.** A circular section carries axial compression equally in every direction, which is what a column needs.

examTip.trap: Lintels and slabs work in bending, where a rectangular section is far more efficient.
examTip.trick: Round for compression, rectangular for bending.

questions.stem: The isometric projection of a circle is:
questions.solution: **An ellipse.** The plane of the circle is inclined to the picture plane, so it foreshortens in one direction and projects as an ellipse.

examTip.trap: It stays a circle only in a view taken normal to its own plane, which isometric never is.
examTip.trick: Tilt a coin and look at it.

questions.stem: Quicklime reacts with water to give:
questions.solution: **Slaked lime.** CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, with a violent release of heat. The hydrated product is slaked lime.

examTip.trap: Carbon dioxide is given off when limestone is calcined — the step before this one.
examTip.trick: Slaking is the addition of water, and the product takes its name from it.

questions.stem: The assessment made before tendering, to check whether a firm can carry out the work, is:
questions.solution: **Pre-qualification.** Pre-qualification screens firms before bids are invited, so only capable contractors tender.

examTip.trap: Post-qualification runs the same checks after bids are opened, on the lowest bidder alone.
examTip.trick: Pre- is before the tender, post- is after it.

questions.stem: The specific gravity of water is:
questions.solution: **1.** Specific gravity is measured against water itself, so water's own value is one by definition.

examTip.trap: 0.001 is the density of water in kilograms per cubic centimetre, and the decimal places invite a guess.
examTip.trick: A ratio of a thing to itself is one.
examTip.mnemonic: Water is the reference, so its own value is one.

questions.stem: The strength of timber is greatest:
questions.solution: **Along the grain.** The fibres run along the grain and carry load in their own direction. Across the grain they need only be prised apart.

examTip.trap: "Equally in all directions" would make timber isotropic, which is the one thing it certainly is not.
examTip.trick: Think of splitting firewood — it parts along the grain, never across it.

questions.stem: The storage capacity required of a reservoir is determined from a:
questions.solution: **Mass curve.** The mass curve accumulates inflow against time, and the largest departure between it and the demand line is the storage needed.

examTip.trap: The flow duration curve shows how often a flow is exceeded, which sizes the plant rather than the reservoir.
examTip.trick: Storage is a volume, so it comes from a cumulative plot.
examTip.mnemonic: Mass curve gives storage; duration curve gives plant size.

questions.stem: The correct order of points on the stress-strain curve of mild steel is:
options: Proportional limit, elastic limit, yield, ultimate, breaking
Elastic limit, proportional limit, yield, ultimate, breaking
Yield, proportional limit, elastic limit, ultimate, breaking
Elastic limit, yield, proportional limit, ultimate, breaking
questions.solution: **Proportional limit, elastic limit, yield, ultimate, breaking.** The curve leaves the straight line first, then stops recovering, then yields, then reaches its peak, then breaks.

examTip.trap: The proportional and elastic limits lie so close together on a real curve that their order is easily reversed.
examTip.trick: Proportionality is lost before elasticity is.

questions.stem: Capillary rise is greatest in:
questions.solution: **Silt.** Rise is inversely proportional to pore size, so the finer the soil the higher it climbs. Silt combines small pores with enough permeability for the water to move.

examTip.trap: Clay has the smallest pores of all, but its permeability is so low that the rise takes months.
examTip.trick: Smaller pores, higher rise — until the water can no longer travel.

questions.stem: The estimated value of a built-up property at the end of its useful life, without being dismantled, is the:
questions.solution: **Salvage value.** Salvage value assumes the asset is sold whole and still has some use. Scrap value assumes it is broken up for materials.

examTip.trap: Scrap value is the near neighbour and differs only in whether the thing is demolished.
examTip.trick: Salvaged things still stand; scrapped things do not.

questions.stem: The most commonly used vertical lift gate is the:
questions.solution: **Fixed-wheel gate.** Wheels on the gate run on rails in the piers, so friction is rolling rather than sliding and a large gate can be raised with modest effort.

examTip.trap: The radial gate is also very common, but it rotates about a trunnion rather than lifting vertically.
examTip.trick: The question says vertical lift, which rules out anything that swings.

questions.stem: The minimum compressive strength of M1 grade mortar is:
questions.solution: **10 N/mm².** Mortar grades are named for their 28-day compressive strength, and M1 is the strongest of the masonry mortars at 10 N/mm².

examTip.trap: The weaker grades are used far more often in ordinary brickwork, so their figures come to mind first.
examTip.trick: The grade letter runs the opposite way to the richness of the mix.

questions.stem: The sum of the weights of all permanent structural and non-structural components of a building is the:
questions.solution: **Dead load.** Dead load is everything permanently there — the structure, the finishes, the partitions and the fixed services.

examTip.trap: Imposed load also acts downwards and is also sustained, but it is the occupancy rather than the fabric.
examTip.trick: If it would still be there in an empty building, it is dead load.

questions.stem: Land treatment of sewage is best suited to:
questions.solution: **Agricultural land.** The effluent irrigates and fertilises the crop while the soil filters and oxidises it, so flat cultivated land with permeable soil suits it.

examTip.trap: A steep slope drains freely, which sounds ideal until the effluent runs off instead of soaking in.
examTip.trick: The land must absorb and use the effluent, not shed it.

questions.stem: A submerged intake is used in a:
questions.solution: **Lake.** Still water lets a submerged intake sit on the bed without obstructing navigation or collecting floating debris.

examTip.trap: A river intake must stay accessible and clear of silt, which a structure on the bed does not.
examTip.trick: Submerged means out of reach, which only still water permits.

questions.stem: A sewer that receives the flow of two or three main sewers and carries it to the treatment works is an:
questions.solution: **Intercepting sewer.** The interceptor runs across the ends of the main sewers and takes their flow away from the watercourse they used to discharge into.

examTip.trap: A combined sewer carries sewage and storm water together — a statement about contents rather than position.
examTip.trick: An interceptor intercepts other sewers, not other flows.

questions.stem: The drain built parallel to a hill road to intercept water flowing down the hillside is a:
questions.solution: **Catch water drain.** It is cut along the hillside above the road and leads the water away before it reaches the formation.

examTip.trap: The side drain is also parallel to the road, but lies beside the carriageway and takes surface water off it.
examTip.trick: The catch drain catches water before it arrives; the side drain removes what already has.
examTip.mnemonic: Catch drain uphill, side drain alongside.

questions.stem: The primary function of a cross regulator is to:
options: Raise the level so the off-taking canal draws its supply
Discharge excess water out of the canal
questions.solution: **Raise the level so the off-taking canal draws its supply.** Built across the parent canal, it heads up the water so the off-take can draw its full share even at low flow.

examTip.trap: A canal escape discharges excess water, and the two structures stand on the same canal.
examTip.trick: To raise a level you must obstruct the main channel.

questions.stem: The declining balance method of depreciation is also known as the:
questions.solution: **Constant percentage method.** The same percentage is written off the remaining book value each year, so the amount falls while the rate stays fixed.

examTip.trap: The straight line method keeps the amount constant instead of the percentage — the exact inverse.
examTip.trick: Constant rate on a falling balance, or constant amount on the original.

questions.stem: A washout (drainage) valve in a pipeline is located at the:
questions.solution: **Lowest point.** Sediment and water both collect at the low points, so that is where the main is drained and flushed.

examTip.trap: An air valve goes at the summit, and the pair are routinely swapped.
examTip.trick: Water runs down, air rises.

questions.stem: The method of virtual work is used to find:
questions.solution: **Deflection.** A unit virtual load is applied at the point and in the direction wanted, and the work equation yields the displacement there.

examTip.trap: Strain energy is what the method is built on, so it reads like the output rather than the tool.
examTip.trick: Apply a unit load where you want the answer.

questions.stem: Whether a solid waste is classed as hazardous does NOT depend on its:
questions.solution: **Colour.** Hazard is judged on what the waste is, how concentrated it is and how much of it there is. Appearance has no bearing.

examTip.trap: Colour is often a sign of contamination, which makes it feel like a criterion.
examTip.trick: Ask which property could not change the harm done.

questions.stem: Shear reinforcement is provided in an RC section to:
options: Counteract the negative moment at the support
Resist diagonal tension and the cracks it causes
questions.solution: **Resist diagonal tension and the cracks it causes.** Shear produces principal tension at about 45°, which concrete cannot carry. Stirrups cross that plane and hold the crack closed.

examTip.trap: Diagonal compression exists in the web too, but concrete is strong in compression and needs no help there.
examTip.trick: Concrete fails in tension, so the steel goes where the tension is.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant is mainly sized on the basis of:
options: The square root of the peak load
questions.solution: **Maximum demand.** The installed capacity must meet the highest demand placed on it; anything less and the plant fails at the peak.

examTip.trap: Average demand decides the energy generated and the revenue, but not the size of the machines.
examTip.trick: Capacity answers the peak; energy answers the average.

questions.stem: The hydraulic gradient line:
options: Is never below the pipe centre line
Always lies below the energy gradient line
Always slopes downward in the direction of flow
Lies above the energy gradient line
questions.solution: **Always lies below the energy gradient line.** The two differ by the velocity head, which is never negative, so the HGL is always the lower of the pair.

examTip.trap: The HGL can fall below the pipe centre line, which is exactly what happens where the pressure is negative.
examTip.trick: EGL = HGL + v²/2g, and the velocity head cannot be negative.

questions.stem: In the Terai, a canal is generally aligned along the:
questions.solution: **Ridge line.** A ridge canal commands land on both sides and crosses no natural drainage, so it needs no cross-drainage works.

examTip.trap: A contour canal is the hill alignment, used where the ground is too steep to follow a ridge.
examTip.trick: Flat country allows the ridge; hill country forces the contour.

questions.stem: Rankine's theory of earth pressure is applied to a:
questions.solution: **Cantilever retaining wall.** Rankine assumes a smooth vertical back, which the virtual back of a cantilever wall provides.

examTip.trap: Coulomb's theory, which allows for friction on an inclined face, is the one used for gravity walls.
examTip.trick: Rankine for a vertical smooth back, Coulomb for anything else.

questions.stem: For a wide rectangular channel, the hydraulic radius is approximately:
questions.solution: **R = y.** R = By/(B + 2y). When B is much larger than y the denominator is nearly B, leaving the depth.

examTip.trap: R = y/2 is the condition for the most economical trapezoidal section — a different result about a different channel.
examTip.trick: Let B tend to infinity and watch the expression collapse.
examTip.mnemonic: Wide channel: R equals the depth.

questions.stem: The capital required to keep an organisation running day to day is:
questions.solution: **Working capital.** Working capital pays wages, materials and running costs between doing the work and being paid for it.

examTip.trap: Mobilisation capital is the advance for setting up site — a one-off at the start rather than a continuing need.
examTip.trick: Working capital is what keeps the business working.

questions.stem: Planning in project management is carried out to:
options: Fix the scheduling technique to be used
Set the objectives and the scope of the project
questions.solution: **Set the objectives and the scope of the project.** Planning decides what is to be achieved and what is included, before scheduling and resourcing can begin.

examTip.trap: Resource allocation and scheduling follow planning, and are loosely called planning in ordinary speech.
examTip.trick: Planning answers what and why; scheduling answers when and who.
examTip.mnemonic: Plan the scope, then schedule it.

questions.stem: A trapezoidal combined footing is used when:
options: The inner column carries more load than the outer one
The outer column carries more load than the inner one
The two columns carry equal loads
questions.solution: **The outer column carries more load than the inner one.** The footing is made wider under the heavier outer column so its centroid falls under the resultant and the pressure stays uniform.

examTip.trap: The reverse case is handled by a rectangular combined footing, and the two are easily transposed.
examTip.trick: The wide end goes under the heavy column.

questions.stem: On Mohr's circle, a principal plane is the point at which the:
questions.solution: **Shear stress is zero.** Principal planes are defined as the planes carrying no shear, which on the circle are the two points on the horizontal axis.

examTip.trap: Maximum shear occurs at the top and bottom of the same circle, 90° away — the other pair of special points.
examTip.trick: Principal means no shear, by definition.

questions.stem: The permissible deflection of a steel beam is generally limited to:
questions.solution: **Span/325.** IS 800 limits the deflection of a simply supported steel beam to span/325 under imposed load.

examTip.trap: Span/250 is the common limit in several other codes and for other materials, which makes it the habitual answer.
examTip.trick: Steel in IS 800 takes the stricter 325.

questions.stem: The pressure difference across the film of a soap bubble of radius R is:
questions.solution: **4T/R.** A bubble has two surfaces, inside and out, so it carries twice the 2T/R of a single-surface droplet.

examTip.trap: 2T/R is the droplet, which has one surface only — the commonest slip in this topic.
examTip.trick: Count the surfaces: droplet one, bubble two.

questions.stem: The speed of a turbine working under a head of 1 m and developing 1 kW is its:
questions.solution: **Specific speed.** Specific speed is defined by that hypothetical unit machine, and it decides which type of turbine suits a given site.

examTip.trap: Synchronous speed is the real running speed, set by the generator poles and the system frequency.
examTip.trick: The definition is a standardisation, not a measurement.

questions.stem: Energy downstream of a dam is dissipated by:
options: A hydraulic jump, a roller bucket or a ski jump
questions.solution: **A hydraulic jump, a roller bucket or a ski jump.** All are stilling arrangements; which is used depends on the tailwater level and the geology of the river bed.

examTip.trap: The hydraulic jump is taught first, so it gets taken for the only one.
examTip.trick: Different tailwater conditions call for different devices.

questions.stem: In a flexible pavement, the wheel load spreads through the layers in the shape of a:
questions.solution: **Truncated cone.** The load spreads outwards with depth from the circular contact area, so the stressed zone widens downwards and the stress falls.

examTip.trap: A rigid pavement spreads the load by slab action over a wide area — a different picture entirely.
examTip.trick: The contact patch is circular and the spread is at an angle.

questions.stem: In a symmetrical I-section, the shear stress is a maximum at the:
questions.solution: **Neutral axis.** Shear stress follows the first moment of the area above the level considered, which is greatest at the neutral axis.

examTip.trap: The web-flange junction shows the sharpest jump in shear stress because the width changes abruptly, but the peak is at the axis.
examTip.trick: Bending stress peaks at the extreme fibre, shear stress at the neutral axis.
examTip.mnemonic: Shear in the middle, bending at the edge.

questions.stem: In pre-tensioned prestressed concrete, the tendons are tensioned:
options: While the concrete is being placed
questions.solution: **Before the concrete is placed.** The wires are stretched against abutments first, the concrete is cast around them, and the force is released into it once the concrete has gained strength.

examTip.trap: Post-tensioning does the opposite — concrete first, tendons stressed through ducts afterwards.
examTip.trick: The prefix says when the tensioning happens relative to the casting.

questions.stem: For a large, rapidly growing city, population is best forecast by the:
questions.solution: **Geometric increase method.** Growth at a constant percentage compounds, which is what a rapidly expanding city does. Arithmetic growth adds a fixed number each decade and suits a settled town.

examTip.trap: The geometric method over-predicts an old, saturated city, which is why the arithmetic method exists at all.
examTip.trick: Fast growth compounds; steady growth adds.

questions.stem: Terzaghi introduced mobilised cohesion and a mobilised friction angle to deal with:
questions.solution: **Local shear failure.** In loose or soft soil the full strength is never mobilised, so c and tan φ are reduced to two-thirds of their values.

examTip.trap: General shear failure is the case the original formula was derived for, and needs no such reduction.
examTip.trick: Loose soil cannot develop its full strength, so the parameters are cut.

questions.stem: In the long wall-short wall method, the length of the long wall is the centre-line length plus:
questions.solution: **One breadth.** Half a breadth is added at each end, which is one full breadth in all; the short wall loses the same amount.

examTip.trap: Half a breadth is what is added at each end, so quoting it as the total counts only one corner.
examTip.trick: Two ends, half a breadth each.
examTip.mnemonic: Long wall gains a whole breadth.

questions.stem: The rise and fall method of reducing levels provides a check on:
questions.solution: **Back, intermediate and fore sights.** Every reading enters the rise or fall column, so the arithmetic check covers them all — which is why it is preferred to the height of instrument method.

examTip.trap: The height of instrument method is quicker but checks only the back and fore sights, leaving intermediates unverified.
examTip.trick: Rise and fall is slower precisely because it uses every reading.

questions.stem: The yield strength of a property class 4.6 bolt is:
questions.solution: **240 N/mm².** The first number is the ultimate strength in hundreds — 400 N/mm² — and the second is the ratio of yield to ultimate: 0.6 × 400 = 240.

examTip.trap: 400 N/mm² is the ultimate strength, which the designation states directly and is the easier number to reach for.
examTip.trick: Multiply the two figures and add a zero: 4 × 6 × 10 = 240.

questions.stem: At the breakpoint in chlorination, the residual chlorine is at its:
questions.solution: **Minimum.** Chloramines formed earlier are destroyed as the dose rises, so the residual falls to a minimum at the breakpoint; beyond it free chlorine appears and the residual climbs again.

examTip.trap: Free chlorine appears after the breakpoint, which makes a maximum feel like the right description of it.
examTip.trick: The curve dips at the breakpoint and then rises.
examTip.mnemonic: The residual dips to a minimum at the breakpoint.

questions.stem: An attracting groyne is one that is:
questions.solution: **Inclined downstream.** Pointing downstream draws the current towards the bank it stands on; pointing upstream repels it away.

examTip.trap: The repelling groyne is the mirror image, and which way round they go is the whole question.
examTip.trick: The groyne points the way the water is led.
